description: Strange Loop talks from Strange Loop 2022.

talks.title: "Expert Software Developers' Approach to Error" by Marian Petre (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents expert Software Developers Approach to Error by Marian Petre (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Marian Petre presents at Strange Loop 2022 on how expert software developers treat errors as opportunities rather than nuisances to be quickly swatted away.

Key Topics: Contrasting novice bug-fixing with expert approaches; errors as signals of deeper design flaws; recognizing bug clusters indicating systemic issues; and building cultures that embrace investigative debugging.

Technical Details: Petre describes how experts pause at anomalies, asking why rather than immediately patching. They examine dependencies and code structure to determine whether a bug indicates architectural misconceptions.

Takeaways: Expert developers use errors as learning inputs. Teams should cultivate curiosity about anomalies and resist pressure to ship quick fixes that mask underlying design problems.

talks.title: "The Early Days of id Software: Programming Principles" by John Romero (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Provides the Early Days of id Software: Programming Principles by John Romero (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
John Romero opens with the early years of id Software, from his teenage programming on the Apple II and his time at Softdisc alongside John Carmack. A smooth-scrolling PC demo led to the Commander Keen trilogy, made in three months in 1990, and the company's first engine licensing deal. He then walks through the studio's releases, from Wolfenstein 3D and Doom to Quake, and how a very small team kept up the pace.

The middle of the talk covers the principles the team followed. They avoided prototypes and kept code shippable at all times, and made the engine fall back to defaults when data failed to load so the game always ran. They built strong internal tools, developed Doom on NeXT workstations rather than DOS, and tested their own work heavily instead of passing bugs to testers. Romero also describes a Doom freeze that Carmack solved by reasoning about a 16-bit timer counter without debugging. Early collaboration relied on floppies and a Novell file server, with no source control until much later.

In the question session, Romero explains the company's equal-share ownership arrangement, its habit of keeping earnings in the bank, and hiring based on passion and personality fit. For practitioners, the takeaways are to keep builds runnable, test your own code aggressively, communicate closely within a team, and invest in tools that speed iteration. He contrasts this with modern game development, where teams build prototype "gym" levels to test each feature before combining them.

talks.title: "Leveraging AI for Global Health" by África Periañez (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents leveraging AI for Global Health by África Periañez (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Global Health Context

África Periañez presents Bonsai, a Gates Foundation-funded organization bringing AI and machine learning to underserved communities. She cites stark health disparities—few doctors per capita in low-income countries and high preventable maternal mortality.

Behavioral Change Mission

Bonsai focuses on patient and provider engagement rather than raw prediction. Medication only helps if people take it and supplies exist locally, so the organization nudges behaviors toward better health outcomes using digital data.

Team Origins and Naming

Leadership backgrounds come from video-game machine learning that modeled individual player engagement. The name references Japanese benshi narrators who explained silent films—Bonsai aims to reveal what is hidden in health data.

Technical Platform

The platform organizes mobile-generated health data in low-connectivity regions, runs randomized trials and reinforcement-learning bandits, and builds recommendation, censoring, and forecasting models aimed at actionable interventions rather than prediction alone.

talks.title: "Stop Writing Dead Programs" by Jack Rusher (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Provides stop Writing Dead Programs by Jack Rusher (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Thesis

Jack Rusher's Strange Loop talk Stop Writing Dead Programs revives Seymour Papert's critique that computing education—and much of industry—still perpetuates irrational, historically inherited practices.

Punch-card era

Rusher recounts Fortran on punch cards, VAX batch jobs, 45-minute feedback loops, and terminal fear of dropped decks—hard in dumb ways unrelated to the actual problem, rewarding a priesthood with strong working memory.

Modern parallels

Today's long compile cycles, Docker/CI deploy waits, and cloud batch pipelines echo the same slow feedback; Docker exists partly because underlying stacks are overly complex.

Wrong mental model

Compile-run separation, linear single-threaded execution, and input-output-transformer programs poorly fit long-lived servers (1000-day uptimes) and rich GUI/event-driven systems we actually build.

Call to action

Mastering pointlessly hard workflows breeds pride in preserving them; Rusher urges abandoning dead program thinking for interactive, pragmatic development environments.

talks.title: "Programmable Ink" by Szymon Kaliski (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Discusses programmable Ink by Szymon Kaliski (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Dynamic Medium, Static Tools

Szymon Kaliski of Ink & Switch presents "Programmable Ink" at Strange Loop, questioning why digital drawing tools simulate paper instead of exploiting computation. Even sophisticated paint programs remain static regarding behavior—you cannot sketch seating charts that reorder when guests RSVP or bookshelves that parametrize after drawing.

## Tyranny of Formalisms

Professional design software demands pixel perfection early, pulling creators into rigid workflows. Kaliski argues the dynamic medium should blend sketching freedom with programmable behavior, avoiding premature commitment to final layouts.

## Spatial Queries Prototype

Demonstrations introduce spatial queries: canvas regions that ask which objects overlap them, returning live lists bound to UI properties. Drawing a checkbox near queried zones toggles state bidirectionally—mark removal clears lists; new marks repopulate them. Lists convert to Boolean conditions driving other elements.

## Research Toward Programmable Sketching

Programmable Ink prototypes explore how informal diagrams gain reactive logic without traditional coding. The research track targets creators who think visually first, enabling iterative exploration where hand-drawn structures carry executable semantics—a middle ground between whiteboards and production CAD systems.

talks.title: "Building Observability for 99% Developers" by Jean Yang (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates building Observability for 99% Developers by Jean Yang (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Jean Yang argues that modern software is a heterogeneous ecosystem of APIs, third-party services and microservices, so no up-front specification or language-level guarantee describes what a system actually does. She says the usual approach of logs, metrics and traces assumes expert teams with time to instrument everything, while many developers inherit systems they did not write and lack the time to set up monitoring.

She describes her team's attempt to build understanding of a system with as little developer effort as possible: no code changes, no annotations and no custom dashboards. The approach uses an eBPF-based agent that passively watches network traffic from outside the data path and builds maps of the API. Early users found the raw traffic overwhelming, so the team shifted toward inferring basic endpoint structure, such as grouping paths that differ only by an ID, instead of richer type and change tracking, which users cared about less. Encrypted traffic remained a hard limit. Her team had tried parsing TLS metadata, offered a proxy to some customers, and was considering building one into the agent.

In the question period she pointed to intrusion detection as a useful precedent, said service meshes lack standardization, and explained why her team focused on smaller teams first. Her main takeaway is that developers need new practices and drop-in tools that work across heterogeneous components and do not require expertise in either the tool or the system. Practitioners should expect that their systems will change faster than their tooling can keep up with.

talks.title: "A Distributed File System for Secure P2P Applications" by Brooklyn Zelenka (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Evaluates A Distributed File System for Secure P2P Applications by Brooklyn Zelenka (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Brooklyn Zelenka, co-founder and CTO of Fission, presents WNFS (Web Native File System)—a distributed file system for secure peer-to-peer applications built on local-first principles. The three-year project, initially dismissed as impossible, fundamentally inverts traditional server-centric architectures to let users own and control their data across multiple stores while operating offline-first.

## Motivation and Context
Zelenka argues that internet infrastructure has radically changed since the 1990s: clients are now powerful (e.g., iPhone chips), bandwidth is abundant but latency is the constraint, access is distributed globally, and data privacy is increasingly regulated. Yet software architecture remains trapped in the LAMP stack paradigm of centralized servers. WNFS applies newer data structures and leverages modern client capabilities to enable users to own their data, possess one or more stores, and load data into applications as needed—mirroring how native platforms manage resources.

## Four Core Properties
The system requires four properties: local-first Access Control, arbitrary metadata, mutability, and versioning. Each is essential; initial skeptics discover their necessity when exploring how to avoid them.

## Public File System: Content Addressing and Hashing
The foundation uses content addressing—hashing data (e.g., SHA-256) so that identical content produces identical hashes deterministically. This differs from traditional URL-based addressing (which is location-dependent). Content addresses enable deterministic naming across distributed systems, selective replication, and clean diffs. WNFS uses IPLD (Interplanetary Linked Data) format with bytes and links. A mutable pointer (DNS TXT records) decouples addressing from data structures, permitting updates, atomic writes, and rollbacks while preserving history.

## File System Structure
The layout includes: a root with owner information (public key), public content, encrypted data sections, and a sharing inbox. Public files are organized in Merkle trees: each file has a header (SDK-controlled), raw user data, and metadata; directories index files and subdirectories. Changes create new versions; shared unchanged blocks enable structural sharing. History is stored per file as a linear or branched sequence; revisions form a causal semi-lattice supporting merging. A tunable hash-based checkpoint mechanism accelerates diffs by identifying the last common ancestor across branching histories.

## Private File System: The Dark Forest
Encrypted data is organized in a CHAMP (Compact Hash Array Map Prefix tree)—an optimized hash-array map trie with branching factor 16, balancing efficient diffs and shallow trees. The structure is append-only, miracleized (identical structures have identical hashes), and concurrency-friendly. All leaves appear as random bits, enabling efficient merging via set union. Every block and file has a unique key, derived randomly and unrelated to hierarchy; this prevents key rotation from affecting unrelated files. Users decrypt blocks starting from one top key, progressively discovering the tree structure—no server is queried for access proofs.

## Temporal Cryptography and Access Control
Time is orthogonal to hierarchy. A key ratchet—repeatedly hashing a key to derive the next version's key—enables forward traversal in time but not backward. A skip ratchet permits efficient jumps. Granular access is provided by deriving keys: giving access to a specific file, directory, or time range creates zero-knowledge witnesses using RSA accumulators with quasi-commutativity. These accumulators hash path segments and version information together in an order-agnostic way (quasi-commutative), proving membership without revealing the path.

## Write Access and Lazy Rooting
Users with partial write access create updates unrooted to the top (because the top structure is unknown to them). These are lazily attached upward when someone with higher access integrates them, performing structural sharing and backlinks. Over time, the tree is collaboratively built from leaf to root.

## Path Privacy
To prevent correlation attacks (e.g., identifying legal vs. family documents), all file names and paths are encrypted. The system uses RSA accumulators to prove that a file name exists under a given parent without revealing either the hierarchy or the name itself—just opaque random bits and a witness.

## Technical Implementation
Originally written in TypeScript, WNFS is being rewritten in WebAssembly and Rust to target web and native applications. The system emphasizes that "all pipes are broken"—assuming data will be compromised, so encryption-at-rest and in-transit is mandatory. The API mirrors Unix commands (ls, mkdir, rm, mv) with additions for history, versioning, and merge semantics.

## Use Cases and Future Work
Deployed for web apps (Dropbox clones), tools for thought (TiddlyWiki), data science, and storage network integration. Future work includes completing the WebAssembly rewrite, building local-first encrypted collaborative data logs, expressing CRDTs as data log, improving IPFS networking (batching requests, maintaining peer connections), and deploying zero-knowledge proofs for certificate privacy. The project is driving standards via the Web Native File System working group spec.

## Key Takeaways
Content addressing and Merkle trees provide security and efficient caching. Structural sharing across versions saves space while preserving history and enabling rollbacks. Temporal cryptography separates time-based access from hierarchy. Path privacy via accumulators prevents correlation attacks. Lazy rooting enables offline-first collaboration. The system scales from local use to global peer-to-peer networks while maintaining end-to-end encryption and user data ownership.

talks.title: "Avoiding the Pitfalls of Autoscaling with Constant Work" by David Grizzanti (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Investigates avoiding the Pitfalls of Autoscaling with Constant Work by David Grizzanti (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk examines where standard autoscaling breaks down in distributed systems. Drawing on his platform work at Comcast, the speaker covers cascading failures: unbounded request volume that saturates new capacity, regional failovers that overload a second region, and long startup times that leave new instances unready while traffic piles onto the rest. Mitigations include capping requests per instance, controlling failover load, and keeping warm standby capacity.

The middle section introduces constant work, where a system does the same amount and type of work whatever the load. Examples from AWS include Route 53 health checkers that probe on a fixed schedule without retrying failures and publish full state each time, and load balancer control planes that poll configuration at a fixed interval. The speaker links this to anti-fragility, the idea that a system can gain from stress, and contrasts it with robust and resilient designs.

The hands-on part compares push and pull metrics collection using Prometheus and the Avalanche load generator on EC2 and ECS. Pull scraping gave clear visibility but needed manual reconfiguration, while pushing metrics into a single Prometheus server overwhelmed it once senders scaled up. Running Prometheus in agent mode, scraping locally and remote-writing to a backend, avoids slow recovery from write-ahead logs and keeps alerting close to services. The takeaway is to look for constant-work patterns that ease scaling and to design for stress, not just steady load.

talks.title: "Level Up Your Machine Learning Lifecycle" by Yaqi Chen (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Investigates level Up Your Machine Learning Lifecycle by Yaqi Chen (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the struggle to deliver machine learning work across industries such as agriculture, healthcare and transportation, where data sources differ and people who know both data science and a specific domain are scarce. The speaker frames the machine learning lifecycle as data, model and deployment stages that apply everywhere, even when the inputs change.

A pet-food case sorts photos of cats and dogs. Images are center-cropped, resized to a fixed input size, split randomly 80/20 into training and test sets to avoid leakage, and then used to train a convolutional network. A vehicle identification case reads license plates, a much smaller target. The team reused the same pipeline by adding a region proposal step based on random crops, then repeated the resize, split and training steps. This led to a productized image and object detection workflow with a central configuration step, sensible defaults, and handlers for on-premises or cloud storage. Segmentation needs pixel-level work and sits in a separate product.

Practical takeaways include agreeing on a standard format for model inputs and outputs so handoffs between data scientists and engineers go smoothly, and involving both groups early in data design. Small modules are unit tested with pytest, and teams should set monitoring cadence and thresholds after deployment. The talk closes with trends toward low-code tools and human-in-the-loop review, where people can override model decisions.

talks.title: "Hodor: Detecting and Addressing Overload in LinkedIn Microservices" by Bryan Barkley
talks.teaser: Reviews hodor: Detecting and Addressing Overload in LinkedIn Microservices by Bryan Barkley and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Hodor (Holistic Overload Detection and Overload Remediation) is a system developed by LinkedIn to detect and address overload conditions in microservices. Deployed to approximately 1000 services in production for over a year, Hodor has engaged in hundreds of instances to protect services from becoming overloaded and unresponsive.

Barkley defines overload as when a process is asked to do more work than it can handle with available resources. Resources fall into two categories: physical (CPU, memory, disk IO, network bandwidth—hardware-limited) and virtual (thread pools, connection pools, file descriptors, semaphores—configurable thresholds that still cause system-wide overload when exceeded). Common scenarios include traffic spikes, back pressure from slow downstream services causing upstream accumulation, and noisy neighbors on the same host impacting each other.

Hodor uses three primary detectors with conservative thresholds. The Heartbeat/CPU Detector monitors JVM thread scheduling delays by running a background thread that sleeps for ~10ms; consistent violations (e.g., 28+ violations in 30 windows) indicate CPU starvation. The Garbage Collection Detector tracks time spent in GC and fires on thresholds like >11% GC time for >10 consecutive seconds, indicating potential GC death spirals. The Thread Pool Detector monitors Jetty thread pool queue wait times, flagging overload if requests wait >50ms for >10 consecutive seconds.

Hodor employs multiple load shedding strategies. Initial Adaptive Percentage approach dropped fixed traffic percentages but proved inefficient with varying patterns. Concurrency-Based strategy dynamically limits concurrent requests, better handling traffic fluctuations. Rate-Based with Traffic Tiering uses throughput as the metric with concurrency as the source of truth, enabling three-tier prioritization: optional (pre-fetches, offline systems—dropped first), degradable (user sees some impact), and non-degradable (critical paths—dropped last).

To prevent retry storms, Hodor maintains server-side histograms tracking retry counts and client-side budgets limiting retries. No retry storms have occurred with this system in place. Hodor deployed in batches with load shedding initially disabled, monitoring services for at least one week through production load tests before enabling. False positives arose from code behavior changes, fleet resizing, and poorly-tuned garbage collection; solutions included correlating detector firings with latency increases using moving average crossover algorithms.

Future roadmap includes additional detectors for Netty event loops and Parsec (LinkedIn's async execution engine); capacity engineering integration; intelligent auto-scaling accounting for cascading failures; and support for stateful and data systems. Hodor operates transparently at the framework level, requiring zero configuration from application teams.

talks.title: "How live music is evolving in a post pandemic world" by Ben Michel (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents how live music is evolving in a post pandemic world by Ben Michel (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Ben Michel opens by framing live music as a shared human activity that recordings and, more recently, pandemic-era distance disrupted. He introduces networked live music, a idea from a Stanford research center describing real-time performance over a computer network, and the work behind it: Chris Chafe's low-latency jacktrip audio streaming, the commercial effort around it, and web audio standards that let browsers synthesize sound.

The core constraint is latency. Each hop across distance adds milliseconds, and a jam-room style setup begins to break down at roughly 300 to 400 miles even with specialized software. Browsers add their own problems, such as audio being suspended when a tab is in the background. Instead of a full jam session, he proposes a relay in which each player hears the performance so far and adds to it, much like a studio overdub chain. He walks through the techniques that make this workable: sampling note events in short chunks, calculating per-client timing offsets with a high-resolution clock, sending MIDI messages over WebSockets, using requestAnimationFrame for steadier timing than JavaScript timers, and tracking real-user latency with observability tools plus synthetic tests in several regions.

He closes with a browser prototype that passes notes between players and can route MIDI input and output to hardware or browser-based synthesizers. A recorded example shows about a five-second delay before played notes return to the performer. The takeaway is that browser-based music is still early and full of variables, but it can be made to feel shared, and the work is worth pursuing for fun as much as for function.

talks.title: "Monad I Love You Now Get Out Of My Type System" by Gjeta Gjyshinca (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates monad practitioners Love You Now Get Out Of enterprise Type System by Gjeta Gjyshinca (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from Strange Loop 2022, Gjeta Gjyshinca (software developer at Morgan Stanley) examines the friction caused by using monadic concurrency abstractions, specifically Scala Futures, in large codebases. Working on a core platform supporting over 12 million lines of Scala and around 1,000 developers, the team aimed to decouple business logic from execution mechanics without forcing developers to deal with invasive type wrappers. Gjyshinca presents "Optimus," Morgan Stanley's internal managed runtime and platform that provides automatic concurrency, batching, and caching through simple annotations rather than type-level monadic acrobatics.

### Key Topics
- **Type-System Pollution via Futures**: In idiomatic Scala, introducing Futures transforms straightforward synchronous code into nested for-comprehensions, sequence-of-futures transformations, and complex nested types (such as `Future[Seq[Try[T]]]`). This leaks execution concerns into API signatures, damages readability, and complicates refactoring.
- **Limitations of Complex Functional Alternatives**: Advanced solutions like free monads and applicatives with effects push execution to the program boundaries via interpreters, but require significant category theory knowledge. In massive commercial codebases with developers from varied backgrounds (such as Java or quantitative finance), these approaches impede velocity and hiring.
- **The Analogy of Managed Runtimes**: Modern languages delegate memory management to runtimes via garbage collection rather than making pointers explicit in the type system (e.g., Eden pointers). Similarly, database engines use declarative languages like SQL to abstract away execution plans, concurrency, and locking without exposing them to user queries.
- **The Optimus Runtime and `@node`**: Optimus introduces the `@node` annotation in Scala. Marking a method with `@node` serves as a contract that the function is referentially transparent, allowing the runtime to handle concurrency, I/O batching, and caching automatically while keeping standard return types intact.

### Technical Details
- **Compile-Time Transformations**: The `@node` annotation triggers a Scala compiler plugin that uses `scala-async` techniques to transform annotated methods into state machines at compile time.
- **Runtime Scheduling & Batching**: At runtime, a custom scheduler executes these state machines. While awaiting I/O calls, the scheduler keeps the CPU active and aggregates independent database queries into batched operations, which significantly reduces network roundtrips.
- **Referential Transparency and Caching**: The runtime pairs referential transparency with append-only, bi-temporal data stores. Because querying at a fixed point in time guarantees deterministic results, Optimus transparently caches repeated queries without making redundant database calls.
- **Ecosystem Challenges & Tooling**: Omitting monadic types from method signatures means synchronous methods can inadvertently sit between `@node` calls, creating serialized execution bottlenecks. The platform addresses this through compiler warnings and profilers, while exploring lightweight JVM threads (Project Loom) to dispatch threads cleanly without blocking execution threads.

### Takeaways
Optimus demonstrates that concurrency, caching, and batching can be delegated to a smart runtime rather than burdening the type system. By relying on referential transparency guarantees via simple metadata (`@node`), teams can write concise, declarative business logic while achieving high-throughput, non-blocking parallel execution. Morgan Stanley has been working to open-source the platform (initially nicknamed Optimus Prime) after decoupling proprietary components and renaming packages.

talks.title: "Art you can make by spying on yourself with your phone" by Kate Hollenbach (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates art you can make by spying on yourself with your phone by Kate Hollenbach (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Kate Hollenbach, a media artist and programmer, presents a series of works that examine how phones sense and record their users. She starts from the observation that a phone, with its front and back cameras, GPS and microphones, models the body in far more detail than a mouse does. She built an Android app that recorded video from both cameras each time the phone was unlocked, and later added screen capture.

Over a month she gathered about 1,100 clips. The first installation laid them out across five projectors, and a later 24-hour piece replayed them at the times they were recorded, leaving the last frame behind as a trace. A version called user is present combined front camera, back camera and screen footage into one composite. She then made video portraits of three friends, who filtered their own recordings before the show, and one segment was removed at a mutual friend's request. Participants' reactions varied, with one saying the work made them more wary of surveillance.

The talk ends with ideas for future work: what the project would reveal if it recorded all the time, including while locked, and an audio project that turns 24 hours of recorded speech into text for a generative book. The practical takeaway is that everyday devices capture intimate detail about users and bystanders, and that building your own tools lets you see those limits. Hollenbach also described her build as trial and error, with ffmpeg and Processing handling the frame processing.

talks.title: "Demystifying Privacy Preserving Computing" by Tejas Chopra (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates demystifying Privacy Preserving Computing by Tejas Chopra (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from Strange Loop 2022, Tejas Chopra, a senior software engineer at Netflix, demystifies privacy-preserving computation. The presentation explores how modern systems can perform meaningful computation and machine learning over private data without sacrificing confidentiality. Chopra outlines the tension between full privacy (no data sharing, zero utility) and full utility (unrestricted data exposure, zero privacy), motivating the need for middle-ground techniques that allow organizations to compute over sensitive data safely in domains like healthcare, cloud computing, and blockchain.

### Key Topics
Chopra categorizes privacy-preserving computation into four foundational paradigms:
- **Federated Learning:** Pushing machine learning models to edge devices (e.g., Apple Siri, Google keyboard autocompletion) rather than aggregating raw user data centrally. Devices train models locally and return only updated parameters.
- **Differential Privacy:** A formal mathematical framework that quantifies privacy loss (measured by epsilon) by ensuring the presence or absence of a single individual's record does not significantly alter aggregate query results, typically achieved by injecting calibrated noise.
- **Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC):** Protocols enabling multiple parties to jointly evaluate functions across distributed secret shares without revealing private inputs to any participant, often leveraging Shamir's Secret Sharing.
- **Homomorphic Encryption:** Cryptographic schemes allowing mathematical operations directly on encrypted ciphertexts, producing an encrypted result that decrypts to the plaintext answer.

### Technical Details
- **Federated Learning Trade-offs:** While compliant with privacy regulations like GDPR, it faces device-level compute disparities and "leaky abstractions," where adversaries can reverse-engineer models or infer sensitive data by sniffing updated parameters.
- **Differential Privacy & Epsilon:** Differential privacy bounds individual impact through an epsilon (ε) threshold. While used by organizations like the U.S. Census Bureau (2020), Google Chrome, and Microsoft, researchers identified issues with transparency, citing cases where Apple utilized very high epsilon values that leaked more privacy than anticipated.
- **SMPC & Shamir's Secret Sharing:** SMPC uses polynomial interpolation where a degree-t polynomial hides a secret at $x=0$. It requires at least $t+1$ points to reconstruct the secret, making it information-theoretically secure against unbounded or quantum computing attacks. However, SMPC suffers from high communication latency among nodes and vulnerability to colluding or malicious parties.
- **Homomorphic Encryption Challenges:** Schemes span partial (limited operations), somewhat (limited depth due to accumulating noise), and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). FHE focuses primarily on addition and multiplication, analogous to universal logic gates. IBM's HElib historically ran a trillion times slower than plaintext (reduced to ~75x slower), while Microsoft developed the SEAL library. Noise accumulation remains the central technical challenge during multiplication, requiring noise-resetting mechanisms.
- **Blockchain and Zero-Knowledge Proofs:** During the Q&A, Chopra highlights privacy gaps in public ledgers, noting privacy blockchains like Zcash transitioning from ZK-SNARKs (which required complex trusted setup phases) toward ZK-STARKs to preserve transactional confidentiality.

### Takeaways
Privacy-preserving technologies are not a substitute for core security and authentication; they operate as authorization and data-protection layers. The current adoption of SMPC and FHE is constrained by high computational overhead, communication latency, poor interoperability, and lack of standardized benchmarking across libraries. The future of privacy-preserving systems lies in hybrid architectures—combining SMPC for distributed processing, FHE for encrypted computation, and differential privacy to quantify disclosure risks.

talks.title: "How Automated Tools Can Communicate Effective Strategies for Fixing Bugs" by Justin Smith
talks.teaser: Outlines how Automated Tools Can Communicate Effective Strategies for Fixing Bugs by Justin Smith and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary: Justin Smith describes MatchingRef, a research system that elevates defect reports from one-off fixes to reusable repair strategies. He walks through a novice type-mismatch mistake where copying a Stack Overflow snippet worsens the code because the compiler error lacks explanatory context. MatchingRef analyzes the failing program, infers root causes such as assignment versus return-type mismatches, and surfaces expert strategies instead of literal patch text. He shows mock-ups extending the idea to path-traversal findings so security learners see pattern-level guidance. The talk argues that static analyzers, linters, and compilers should teach higher-level problem solving rather than stopping at red error flags.

talks.title: "How to Recommend Tools for Finding and Fixing Software Errors" by Chris Brown
talks.teaser: Details how to Recommend Tools for Finding and Fixing Software Errors by Chris Brown and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Chris Brown opens with why locating and repairing bugs is difficult, and why the tools built to help are often more frustrating to adopt than working by hand. Using the three wise monkeys as a frame, he describes three approaches his group tried. Automated emails recommending Python static analysis tools drew more complaints than adoptions. Automated GitHub pull requests adding a static analysis tool to Java Maven projects fared no better, since developers saw broken builds, longer build times and new errors.

Peer recommendation worked best. In a follow-up study where paired participants worked on tasks, half of one partner's recommendations led the other to adopt the tool, far above the near-zero rate for emails and pull requests. Yet peer exchange is the least common discovery route and is declining. Brown then turns to nudge theory and proposes a developer recommendation choice architecture built on actionability, feedback and locality. A survey of developers across companies and stacks found that all respondents preferred an actionable recommendation over a static one. His group is building a bot that suggests fixes on GitHub pull requests, though he stresses that whether the approach works in practice is still unproven.

For researchers and toolmakers, he urges fewer false positives and integration into existing workflows instead of interruptions. For developers, he recommends sharing useful tools with colleagues, trialing one during a sprint, and giving feedback during tool evaluations.

talks.title: "Interactive Debugging and Testing Support for Deep Learning" by Tianyi Zhang
talks.teaser: Evaluates interactive Debugging and Testing Support for Deep Learning by Tianyi Zhang and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Deep learning systems differ from traditional software because their logic is learned from training data rather than written by hand, and their internals are high-dimensional arrays that do not fit the breakpoint-and-step approach developers rely on. The speaker illustrates this with a recurrent neural network that classifies comments as positive or negative and wrongly labels a clearly negative comment as positive.

To make such a model inspectable, the speaker presents DeepSeer, which abstracts a recurrent network into a finite state machine. Each word of the input moves the model between states, and developers can open a state to see the frequent words and phrases associated with it. Entering the misclassified comment produces a state trace, colored red for negative and blue for positive, showing that the model flipped to positive right after the word "quarters" and never flipped back. Searching the training data for that word revealed that 27 of 28 sentences containing it were labeled positive, pointing to a spurious correlation as the likely root cause.

A user study with 28 computer science students compared DeepSeer against another popular deep learning debugging tool. Students using DeepSeer gave more reasonable root-cause explanations and identified more error-inducing keywords. The takeaway is that developers should take responsibility for model errors and build debugging tools that translate model internals into concepts programmers already understand.

talks.title: "Data Driven Investigation in Defense of Human Rights" by Christo Buschek (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents data Driven Investigation in Defense of Human Rights by Christo Buschek (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces data-driven investigation, a practice where datasets and computational methods drive an inquiry rather than only illustrate it. Buschek walks through earlier examples: the Panama Papers leak, ProPublica's analysis of risk assessment scores in US courts, and the Syrian Archive, which preserves millions of videos and posts documenting the war in Syria.

The main case is the Built to Last investigation into detention camps in Xinjiang. Starting with little public information, the team noticed that map imagery showed censored tiles over some camps. Buschek built a browser-automation scraper that pans across the province and logs masked tiles. It ran for about six weeks on 25 machines and produced over 50 million tile locations, roughly five million of them censored. Cross-referencing those with roads, railways and urban areas cut the set to around 800,000 candidates. Verification then relied on a simple review interface and satellite imagery, where camp features such as walls, guard towers and facilities were identified, plus a blogger's video footage that showed the sites on the ground.

The talk closes with practical lessons: keep your own copy of data because sources disappear, verify only the subset that supports a claim, and expect tools to be short-lived while methods last. Buschek argues that tools carry values around security, privacy, accuracy and maintenance, and that collaboration across programmers, journalists and architects is essential.

talks.title: "Reviving 1990's Digital Dress-Up Dolls with Smooch" by Libby Horacek (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents reviving 1990s Digital Dress-Up Dolls with Smooch by Libby Horacek (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Libby Horacek introduces Kiss, an open specification for digital dress-up dolls that began in 1991 on a Japanese bulletin board system. Keeping the viewer separate from the doll assets kept files small, and indexed-color cell images shared a single palette per doll, so recoloring meant swapping one file. The configuration file tied everything together, and archives were bundled with LHA compression. She traces the 1995 arrival of F-Kiss, which added animation, sound and scripting, the boom in the early 2000s, and the decline after 2006 as operating systems changed and easier alternatives appeared.

Horacek argues the format is worth reviving for nostalgia, as a record of internet culture, and because its documentation is open. Her viewer, Smooch, has a Haskell back end that unpacks uploads, parses the configuration file with a parser combinator library, and converts cells to PNG, with test-driven development guided by the spec. The front end uses plain JavaScript. Clickable clothing relies on a ghost canvas, where each item is drawn in a unique color so a click can be mapped back to the item beneath it, after simpler image and canvas approaches failed on transparent areas.

She closes with a demonstration of F-Kiss event-based scripting, including a blinking loop built from timers and show or hide actions, and explains how those events map to JavaScript custom events, with timers proving the hardest part. Future ideas include accepting PNG uploads, since artists rarely work in indexed color, and building open-source tools with more contributors.

talks.title: "The Education of a Civic Technologist" by Alex Allain (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Discusses the Education of a Civic Technologist by Alex Allain (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Alex Allain, CTO of U.S. Digital Response, uses his nonprofit's work to explain civic technology, meaning the use of technology to help governments serve the public. The organization matches volunteer technologists with public servants who need help scoping problems and building tools. He presents three projects and keeps the focus on lessons that apply beyond government rather than on deep technical detail.

The first project was a free COVID testing program in Seattle. Volunteers built a multilingual sign-up and reminder system, shared a working demo within days, and helped the city launch in about three weeks; the city later tested over a million people. The lessons were to show a demo rather than lengthy documents and to plan early for who will maintain the software. In Memphis, a team built an emergency rental assistance workflow from scratch with low-code tools such as Jotform, Airtable and Zapier, including automated landlord notices, and got about $13 million to thousands of renters before most places had paid out. There the lessons were building alongside government staff and working with the urgency of the moment.

The third project helped Harris County, Texas, recruit students as poll workers for the 2020 election, using an Airtable application with automated emails and guardian waivers. The approach won a federal award and spread to other counties, one of which later built inventory tracking on top of it. The lesson was to understand each government's window for adopting a new tool. Alex closes by pointing listeners to volunteering with his group, Code for America brigades and public-sector job boards, and notes that choosing established tools with data export helps manage long-term risk.

talks.title: "Modern B-Tree techniques" by Dmitrii Dolgov (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Evaluates modern B-Tree techniques by Dmitrii Dolgov (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
This talk reviews B+ tree indexes, the structure behind most database indexes, and argues that they remain an active research topic rather than a static one. It opens with the RUM conjecture, which holds that an index can optimize at most two of read cost, write cost and memory footprint. The talk then explains the layout: inner pages hold separator keys and child pointers, leaves hold the data, sibling links support range and backward scans, and page splits keep the tree balanced.

Next the speaker covers optimizations within a page. These include key normalization, prefix truncation using fence keys, dynamic prefix truncation at lookup time, choosing split points so separator keys stay short, and storing prefix bytes in the indirection vector to skip comparisons. The talk then surveys variants that change the tree's shape or update path: partitioned B-trees that speed up index creation, hot and cold designs that merge a small mutable tree into an immutable one, hybrid indexes that use Bloom filters, Bw-trees that append delta records and install them with compare-and-swap, and a design for persistent memory. Learned indexes close the survey, where piecewise linear models replace part of the tree.

The closing section notes that many of these designs still keep a tree underneath, and that keeping pages close together reduces TLB pressure. Audience questions covered encrypted data, which makes page-level optimizations hard to apply, and how key distribution relates to tree balance. The takeaway is that index trade-offs should be chosen for the workload, and the speaker points to research papers and a database internals book for further reading.

talks.title: "Sniffing the Metaverse" by Benjamin Cabé (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Examines sniffing the Metaverse by Benjamin Cabé (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Benjamin Cabé argues the metaverse need not be social, three-dimensional, or built on virtual reality. He treats it mainly as industrial plumbing, where sensor and device data flows into existing IT systems so people can interpret it and act on it. His example is remote maintenance on a bottling line: a vibration sensor flags a likely fault and the right technician is alerted. The building blocks he lists are ontologies to describe assets and people, time-series and graph databases to store and query them, and shared standards so readings in different units can be combined.

On the device side, he argues that small sensors should send insights instead of raw data. He walks through a tinyML project in which a low-cost gas sensor feeds summary features into a small neural network on a microcontroller. The network classifies smells such as coffee or whiskey and reports its confidence to the cloud. A student adapted the same framework to detect markers of fungal pneumonia in breath. He also covers spatial anchors, which combine Wi-Fi signal strength, Bluetooth beacons, and motion data to locate points indoors where GPS fails.

A HoloLens demo overlays a building model and the live smell classification. He is candid about the sensor's limited accuracy, and says recognising more smells would need a larger model. He closes by pointing to open-source code and hardware designs and calling for labelled smell datasets. The takeaway is that the metaverse depends on interoperable data more than on any single technology.

talks.title: "Diagrammar: Simply Make Interactive Diagrams" by Pontus Granström (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Explores diagrammar: Simply Make Interactive Diagrams by Pontus Granström (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Pontus Granström, who works at Brilliant, a company that builds bite-sized online STEM lessons, explains why the company built Diagrammer, an in-house tool for making interactive technical diagrams. He describes the limits of the earlier workflow: external tools such as matplotlib, Mathematica and 3D modelling software produced static exports with inconsistent styling, and the internal plotting tools were designed for graphs rather than diagrams.

Diagrammer is written in Elm, a pure functional language, so each diagram is a function from an input value to a picture. Granström walks through a short build of geometric shapes, covering circles, regular polygons, rows, columns, alignment and translation. He then builds a Sierpinski triangle, first by hand and then recursively with a depth parameter, and connects that parameter to a slider so learners can explore each level. Other inputs shown include a two-dimensional locator for positioning objects and a stepper for moving through animations one step at a time.

He argues that the design favours clarity: named functions that say what they do, vectors as a core type, no hidden global state, and a deliberately small, curated set of building blocks, styles and interactions. This keeps lesson diagrams consistent, precise and interactive without requiring authors to be designers. The talk closes by stressing that diagrams suit STEM teaching better than plotting in many cases, and that a focused tool is more approachable and more likely to inspire creative use.

talks.title: "There Are No Shortcuts in Organizing, but Technology Sure Does Help" by
talks.teaser: Details there Are No Shortcuts in Organizing, but Technology Sure Does Help by Vicki Crosson, Shane Moore and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Shane and Vicki, software engineers at the New York Times, describe how they organized the largest union of tech workers in the country over two and a half years. While emphasizing that "there are no shortcuts in organizing"—requiring thousands of one-on-one conversations—they showcase how custom-built technology provided strategic speed boosts to their campaign.

## Key Technologies Built

**Bubble Chart Generator**: The team created a visualization tool to map union support across the organization. Starting with a spreadsheet tracking 600+ employees using a five-point assessment system (ranging from "all in" to "anti-union"), Shane wrote Python processors to feed data into D3 visualizations with color coding (green for pro-union, red for anti-union, gray for unassessed). Coworker Shea significantly improved the design by removing manager nodes, making the chart far more readable. This eventually evolved into an online interface for uploading CSVs.

**Website**: Built with Next.js and Netlify CMS, the website enabled both developers and non-developers to contribute content. It used static site generation deployed to Netlify's CDN for global availability and speed. The CMS proved accessible enough that people without coding experience could edit testimonials, FAQs with markdown support, and other content.

**Slack Avatar Generator**: Olav created a minimal web app (just static files, no server/database) that let members upload photos and automatically add a union frame. The simplicity sparked organic collaboration—other engineers and designers jumped in unprompted to enhance the tool, enabling live previews of different photos. During remote-only work, seeing widespread adoption in Slack channels became a powerful morale booster and visibility tool.

**Live Vote Count Tracker**: For the NLRB vote, the team added a real-time vote counter to their website using Firebase Realtime Database. During the actual vote, manually typed values were updated as envelopes were read (Shane admits to making one typo that showed they won by three times their actual margin). The tracker included confetti animation, activated by clicking a Tada emoji.

## Technical Approaches

The team prioritized accessibility and ease of contribution. They chose Next.js because most developers at the Times already knew React. Netlify CMS provided a user-friendly interface for non-technical contributors. All code was eventually open-sourced in a GitHub org for the News Guild of New York.

Organizing challenges shaped technical decisions: they manually collected employee names via a "quilting bee" Zoom calls rather than scraping the internal directory (to avoid drawing management attention prematurely). The Amazon Bessemer warehouse example illustrated why accurate org charts matter—a 4x discrepancy in expected warehouse size nearly derailed their campaign.

## Campaign Phases and Outcomes

The campaign involved three main phases: Stage 0 (building an organizing committee of ~10% of the eventual unit), pre-public organizing (conversations with everyone), and public operations (ongoing steward-led dialogue). Management declined voluntary recognition, so a formal NLRB vote occurred in early 2022, ultimately succeeding. The union then transitioned to contract negotiations.

## Key Takeaways

Despite all technological tools, the speakers emphasize that relationships built through thousands of direct conversations remain irreplaceable. Technology accelerates but cannot substitute human connection. Practical advice for remote organizing includes cold-calling with scripts, starting conversations with intrigue ("something not work-related"), and providing structure ("lesson plans" with themes and talking points) to empower less-experienced organizers. The union's data on member support is kept private for strategic reasons, especially during contract bargaining when priorities matter.
